The Jacobin cuckoo (Clamator jacobinus) lays its eggs in the nests of host species, a brood-parasitic strategy that places particular demands on the developing embryo. Eggs incubated at a temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] yield a hatching period of 11.8 days [ab = 11.8 days], a relatively short incubation duration that is characteristic of many parasitic cuckoos and likely reflects selection for rapid development to give the nestling a competitive advantage over host young. Upon emergence, the altricial nestling has a wet weight at birth of 6 grams [Wwb = 6 grams], a modest mass that is typical for the genus. This initial neonatal mass is notably low compared to the adult body size the bird will eventually attain, highlighting the substantial growth trajectory that must be completed during the nestling phase. The chick is entirely dependent on host parental provisioning from the moment of hatching, a period that involves rapid feather development and mass accumulation as the nestling competes for food with any host offspring present in the nest.

During the course of nestling development, progressive tissue growth and yolk absorption drive a rapid increase in bodily mass. The initial wet weight of a newly laid egg or a very freshly hatched individual is approximately 5.1 grams [Ww0 = approximately 5.1 grams], a value that represents the baseline from which all subsequent mass gain proceeds. This starting point is only slightly below the birth mass, indicating that the transition from egg to hatchling involves minimal net loss of water or energy reserves in this species. The altricial nestling grows steadily within the host nest, and the time since birth at fledging is recorded as 16.5 days [tx = 16.5 days] when the chick is developing under the thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic period, which is an ambient temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This fledging interval is relatively short compared to many other bird species of similar body size, a pattern that may be linked to the selective pressures imposed by the brood-parasitic lifestyle, where a rapid departure from the host nest reduces the risk of detection by the host parents.

The Jacobin cuckoo continues its development through the juvenile and sub-adult stages after achieving independence. The time since birth at puberty, or the age at which gonadal maturation occurs, is approximately 49.5 days [tp = approximately 49.5 days] when the bird is developing under the same active thermal regime of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This relatively early attainment of sexual maturity is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid turnover and early reproductive investment, which is typical of many tropical and subtropical bird species. Following puberty, the young adult enters a phase of territory establishment and host searching, and the time since birth at first brood, marking the age at which the first successful reproductive event occurs, is estimated at 365 days [tR = 365 days] at the same temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This delay between achieving physiological maturity and actually reproducing is common in brood parasites, as individuals must first locate suitable host nests and synchronize their laying cycle with that of the host.

Adult body mass in the Jacobin cuckoo shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a larger ultimate size than males. The ultimate wet weight, or maximum adult body mass, for females is 76 grams [Wwi = 76 grams], while males reach a substantially lower asymptotic mass of 71 grams [Wwi = 71 grams]. This difference of approximately 5 grams is likely related to the energetic demands of egg production and the behavioral role of females in scouting and parasitizing host nests, which may favor a larger body frame for increased mobility and egg-carrying capacity. The few available field data indicate that during a single reproductive event, the female deposits one egg into a host nest [N_R_i = one egg into a host nest], and across the extended breeding season she can complete up to 20 such nesting attempts per year [F_R_i = up to 20 such nesting attempts per year], given the availability of multiple host broods in suitable habitats.

Longevity in the Jacobin cuckoo has been estimated based on comparisons with the more extensively studied common cuckoo (Cuculus canorus), given the paucity of long-term banding data for this species. The maximum lifespan is projected at 4709 days [am = 4709 days] under the thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic period, which is again 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This translates to roughly 13 years, which is a considerable lifespan for a bird of this body size and aligns with the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates observed in tropical and subtropical species that face fewer seasonal environmental extremes. Such extended longevity is also consistent with the species' life history, where a prolonged adult phase allows for many reproductive seasons, each involving the careful timing of egg deposition into the nests of specific host species. The interplay between a rapid juvenile phase, sexual maturation just weeks after fledging, and a potential adult lifespan exceeding a decade is unusual among passerine-sized birds and may reflect the specific selective regime of obligate brood parasitism, where early reproduction carries distinct fitness advantages but adult survival remains high due to low predation pressure in tropical environments.
